entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Nubkheperre Intef, reigning from approximately 1603 to 1594 BCE, was a pivotal Egyptian pharaoh of the Seventeenth Dynasty based in Thebes. His rule occurred during the tumultuous Second Intermediate Period, a fragmented era (c. 1650–1550 BCE) when Egypt was divided, with the Hyksos (Fifteenth Dynasty) controlling Lower Egypt from Avaris and the Theban Seventeenth Dynasty holding sway over Upper Egypt. Intef's significance lies in his role as a unifier and a symbolic figure of Egyptian resistance, actively maintaining a distinct Egyptian identity and preparing the ground for the eventual expulsion of the Hyksos by his successors.

During his nine-year reign, Nubkheperre Intef asserted Theban authority over a considerable portion of Upper Egypt, extending his influence northward towards Abydos. An important stela from Abydos, dating to his third regnal year, details his efforts to restore temples and monuments, underscoring his commitment to traditional Egyptian religious practices and royal legitimacy, even in the face of foreign occupation to the north. His tomb, located in the Dra' Abu el-Naga' necropolis on the West Bank of Thebes, was discovered largely intact, providing valuable insights into the funerary practices and artistic styles of this transitional period, including a well-preserved coffin and burial goods.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Nubkheperre Intef was a crucial figure in maintaining Egyptian sovereignty and cultural identity during the Hyksos occupation, directly contributing to the eventual reunification of Egypt by the Theban dynasty. His reign solidified a power base that enabled the subsequent expulsion of foreign rulers and the establishment of the New Kingdom.
